What is SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle)?

SDLC is a structured process used to develop reliable software applications.

It includes several important stages:

 • Requirement Analysis
 • Planning and Design
 • Software Development
 • Software Testing
 • Deployment
 • Maintenance and Monitoring

Traditional SDLC methodologies help software teams organize development activities, manage risks, and deliver applications systematically.

But what changes when AI Agents participate in these stages?

What is ADLC (Agentic Development Lifecycle)?

ADLC describes an agent-assisted approach to software development.

Instead of depending entirely on manual development tasks, developers can use AI Agents to support planning, coding, testing, debugging, documentation, and deployment workflows.

AI Agents can interpret instructions, interact with development tools, generate code, execute supported tasks, and help developers work through complex problems.

However, human supervision, code review, testing, and security remain essential.

The goal of ADLC is not to eliminate software engineering principles. It's to improve how development work gets done using AI.

SDLC vs ADLC — What's the Difference?

Traditional SDLC focuses on organizing software development into structured stages.

Agentic development introduces AI-powered assistance and automation into those stages.

In this video, we'll explore:

 • Traditional SDLC vs Agentic Development
 • Human-Led vs AI Assisted Workflows
 • AI Agents in Software Engineering
 • Automated Code Generation
 • AI Powered Testing and Debugging
 • Agentic Software Development Tools
 • Human-in-the-Loop Development
 • The Future of AI Assisted Coding

You'll understand how AI Agents can support different stages of software development and why these workflows are gaining attention.

AI Tools for Agentic Software Development

Several AI-powered development tools are making agent-assisted workflows more accessible.

Claude Code: An AI coding agent that can work with codebases and development tools.

OpenAI Codex: An AI coding agent designed to assist with software engineering tasks.

Cursor: An AI-powered code editor with coding assistance and agent capabilities.

OpenCode: An open-source AI coding agent for developer workflows.

Replit: A cloud based development platform offering AI-assisted application building.

Other platforms, including Lovable and Emergent, provide different approaches to AI-assisted application development.

These tools demonstrate how software engineering workflows are evolving.

How AI Agents Are Changing Software Engineering

AI Agents can assist developers with tasks such as:

• Understanding project requirements
• Generating application code
• Refactoring existing code
• Creating unit tests
• Debugging software issues
• Writing technical documentation
• Automating repetitive development tasks
• Supporting deployment workflows

By combining human expertise with AI-assisted development, teams can explore faster iteration and more efficient workflows.

The effectiveness of these systems depends on the tools used, project complexity, and the quality of human oversight.

Is Traditional Coding Becoming Obsolete?

AI coding agents are changing the way developers write and maintain software.

But does that mean software engineers are no longer needed?

Not necessarily.

Developers still need to understand software architecture, system design, security, debugging, testing, and business requirements.

AI Agents can accelerate parts of the development process, but human judgment remains important for building reliable production applications.

The future of software engineering is increasingly about combining development expertise with AI capabilities.

SDLC → ADLC: The Next Evolution of Software Development?

AI Agents are becoming increasingly capable of supporting real software engineering tasks.

From planning and coding to testing and deployment, agent-assisted workflows are creating new opportunities for developers and businesses.

Understanding the differences between traditional SDLC and agentic development can help you prepare for these changes.

videos.title: The $1B Company Fixing AI’s Software Bottleneck
videos.description:
Blacksmith (YC W24) is building a faster cloud for continuous integration (CI), helping developers test and ship code as AI coding tools generate more of it.

As software production accelerates, testing and validation are becoming the new bottleneck. That shift has helped Blacksmith grow 20x over the last year, and the company recently raised a $66 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation.

The founders started as outsiders to DevOps and built their first infrastructure using the same high-performance CPUs found in gaming PCs, renting servers originally designed for Minecraft and Call of Duty. Today, they run a much larger fleet with a team of just 30 people, helping companies cut CI waits from minutes to seconds. 

In this first episode of Built to a Billion, they share how they found the idea, won their first 200 customers, and why faster testing will become even more important as agents write more of the world’s code.

_This episode was recorded on September 8, 2026._

*In this episode, he explains:*
■ *The Rigged System:* Why the last 50 years of “trickle-down economics” is not an economic theory, but a deliberate theft designed to transfer wealth from the middle class to the ultra-rich.
■ *Crony Capitalism:* How monopolies in healthcare and lax campaign finance laws allow corporations to essentially purchase politicians, eliminating true competition and driving up prices for average citizens.
■ *The AI Threat:* Why leaving the development of artificial intelligence entirely to profit-driven billionaires threatens to create mass unemployment without any shared public benefits or worker protections.
■ *False Immigration Choices:* How politicians use extreme border rhetoric to divide voters, when the real solution requires simultaneous border security and clear, legal pathways to citizenship for undocumented residents.
■ *Systemic Overhaul:* Why simply electing new politicians changes nothing unless we first dismantle the corrupt incentive structures of gerrymandering, the two-party system, and unregulated corporate lobbying.
